newsitem.title: TURKEY: OLYMPICS-HISTORICAL SETTING REMAINS ISTANBUL'S STRONGEST CARD.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-HISTORICAL SETTING REMAINS ISTANBUL'S STRONGEST CARD.

text.p: An historical setting astride the Bosphorous remains Istanbul's strongest card as it bids to stage the 2004 Olympic Games.
''Asia already meets Europe in Istanbul,'' says an official slogan. ''We invite other continents to follow suit.''
Bid organisers now believe they have overcome the problems which bedevilled their failed bid for the 2000 Games.
"We looked at all the reasons the bid was not approved last time and we believe we have solved those problems now," said Yalcin Aksoy, general director of Istanbul Olympic Bidding Commitee (IOBC).
Those problems included Istanbul's horrendous traffic, threats of attack from separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels, political volatility and questions over the bid's credibility.
In answer to the traffic problems, Istanbul proposes a compact Games with the majority of events held on one site and a single Olympic village virtually next door.
A new light railway and metro system may at best contain the traffic problem of a city of over 12 million constantly swelled by rural migration.

Getting around the city might be tricky, but Istanbul's globally central location should cut travelling time, and costs, for most visitors to the Games and enable prime time viewing for those staying at home.

"With the broadcasting rights for the games already sold and the Games' financial future fully secure, the IOC can afford to take a chance," said Sinan Erdem, president of Turkey's National Olympic Committee.
Although more than 21,000 people have died in the past 12 years in the fight between the PKK and security forces, Aksoy said this could even benefit the Istanbul bid.
"The Games have got so big nowadays they are a target from terrorists wherever they are, even in Atlanta. At least we have the experience in combating these people," Aksoy said.
Perhaps the biggest difficulty faced by Istanbul in its 2000 bid, though, was its lack of credibility.
"If Berlin says they are going to build a stadium, people immediately believe them. If the Turks say that, they say "Oh really? When? How? What with?"," Aksoy said.

To prove they are serious, the IOBC has embarked on an ambitious construction programme. Two indoor stadia and a pool complex are being built and the contract to construct the main 80,000 capacity Olympic stadium has been put out to tender.

To assure the IOC that the money is there, Turkey's politicians passed a law in 1992 giving the IOBC one percent of national lottery, betting tax and housing fund revenues. It passed with no opposition and one abstention.

This money has so far funded Istanbul's bid and the construction projects with a budget of around $15 million a year. It can be increased fivefold if Istanbul makes it into the final five and would also be boosted with private sponsorship.
The IOBC says political division in Turkey ensures that no combination of parties could possibly have the political will or unite long enough to repeal the law.

Others have their doubts. While the Turks are unquestionably fanatical about soccer and have had successes in weightlifting and wrestling, interest in other sports such as athletics, the mainstay of the games, remains slight.

"Olympism is a way of life. The Turkish people are not yet ready for Olympism. We don't have any Olympic sports, no athletes, no swimmers, no gymnasts, only soccer players," said journalist Hincal Uluc.
Istanbul's backers reply that this is exactly why the city needs the Olympics.
"Half of the population of Istanbul is under 20 years old, 90 percent of them come from poor backgrounds. Only with sport can we motivate them and stop them going the wrong way," Erdem said.
"If the Olympics are really about peace, brotherhood and understanding, then we live in a part of the world that needs this most.''
